newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH SKODA AUTO REVISES DOWNWARD NEW SEDAN OUTPUT.
newsitem.headline: CZECH SKODA AUTO REVISES DOWNWARD NEW SEDAN OUTPUT.

text.p: Volkswagen AG's Czech unit, Skoda Auto a.s., said on Friday production of its new mid-sized Octavia sedan could be less than half the original target, due to technical reasons.

Skoda spokesman Jiri Hrabovsky told Reuters the firm's original production target of 5,000 cars may still be reached, but it is more likely to see between 2,000-5,000 Octavias roll off the assembly line this year.
"If everything was going the way we expected, we could have produced 5,000 or more Octavias this year," he said. "(Now we expect) between 2,000-5,000, we will see how it goes."
Hrabovsky said the original plan was dampenend by several issues related to installation, deliveries of materials and individual component supplies, and overall organisation.
He said the firm was unwilling to compromise on quality in order to meet its original target "despite a possible loss of some clients."

But he added the firm's total production target of some 260,000 vehicles for all of 1996, about a 20 percent increase over the previous year, will be "more or less fulfilled", boosted by its other model, the economy sized Felicia.
He added that the Octavia's 1997 production target remained unchaged at 65,000 units.
Client orders for the Octavia in the Czech Republic have totalled some 15,000 units, of which "one in 20 at the most" can be satisfied immediately, Hrabovsky said.
"The majority of this year's (Octavia) production will supply the domestic market," he said.
Company officials have earlier said that Octavia should help Skoda's total production to rise to 350,000 units next year and 400,000 at the turn of the century after 251,000 cars made this year.
The company lost 1.621 billion crowns last year due to heavy investments into a new factory to build the Octavia, but its officials said the firm should come close to breaking even this year.

Volkswagen, according to a privatisation agreement with the Czech goverment, originally took a stake in Skoda in 1992, and increasing its holdings in Skoda to 70 percent last year from 60.3 percent under the deal.
